judge.actionable_reason: All recommendations are specific, technically correct, and directly actionable by a product team. They include: remove contacts permission from app; delete collected contact data; implement granular consent controls; stop recovery calls/messages to non-obligors; publish data retention policy; provide DPDP-compliant notices; and update privacy policy disclosures. Each recommendation maps precisely to the feature's current practice (requesting contacts at sign-up and using them for recovery outreach) and specifies concrete steps to achieve compliance.
judge.grounded_reason: Every finding is fully supported by the cited passages. Finding 1 correctly cites Para 13(1) of 1728 prohibiting access to contact lists and permitting only one-time camera/microphone/location access for onboarding/KYC. Finding 2 accurately cites Para 13(2)-(4) of 1728 on granular consent, revocation, deletion, purpose disclosure, and third-party sharing restrictions. Finding 3 correctly cites Para 100 of 2158 prohibiting harassment including intrusion on privacy of family members, referees and friends through messages. Finding 4 accurately cites Para 14 of 1729 on data storage policies and Para 8 of 1967 on DPDP erasure rules with correct limitation to Third Schedule classes. Finding 5 correctly cites Rule 3 of 1962 on DPDP notice requirements for itemization and purpose disclosure. Finding 6 accurately cites Para 15 of 1730 on comprehensive privacy policies and third-party disclosure.

1728.heading: Chapter III – Digital Lending › C. Technology and Data Requirement
1728.text:
13. Collection, usage and sharing of data with third parties
(1) An NBFC shall ensure that any collection of data by their DLA and DLA of their
LSP is need-based and with prior and explicit consent of the borrower having
audit trail. In any case, an NBFC shall also ensure that DLA of NBFC / LSP
desist from accessing mobile phone resources like file and media, contact list,
call logs, telephony functions, etc. A one-time access can be taken for camera,
microphone, location or any other facility necessary for the purpose of on-
boarding / KYC requirements only, with the explicit consent of the borrower.
(2) The borrower shall be provided with an option to give or deny consent for use

NBFC / LSP delete / forget the data.

findings.obligation: An NBFC must ensure its digital lending app (and its LSP's app) collects only need-based data with prior, explicit, auditable borrower consent, and must make the app desist from accessing the contact list, call logs, telephony functions and similar phone resources. Only one-time access to camera, microphone or location is allowed, for onboarding/KYC, with explicit consent.
findings.recommendation: Remove the contacts permission from the app and any LSP app. Do not read or store the contact list at sign-up, even with the borrower's consent. Delete any contact data already collected. Limit one-time permissions to onboarding/KYC needs.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: Borrowers must be able to give or deny consent for specific data, restrict disclosure to third parties, set retention, revoke consent already given, and have the NBFC/LSP delete their data. The purpose of consent must be disclosed at every stage, and explicit consent is needed before sharing personal information with third parties, unless a statute or regulation requires the sharing.
findings.recommendation: Remove the bulk contacts permission. Give borrowers granular consent, revocation and deletion controls. State the purpose of each data request at every stage. Obtain explicit consent before sharing data with any third party. Do not use sign-up consent as a basis for contacting third parties about debt.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: An NBFC and its agents must not harass or intimidate any person in debt collection, including acts that humiliate publicly or intrude on the privacy of the debtor's family members, referees and friends, or sending inappropriate messages by mobile or social media. Contacting people in the borrower's phone contacts to tell them the borrower owes money is such an intrusion.
findings.recommendation: Stop recovery calls and messages to contact-list persons who are not guarantors or co-obligors. Limit recovery communications to the borrower and legally bound parties. Train and monitor recovery staff and agents accordingly.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: The NBFC must have clear data-storage policy guidelines covering the type of data stored, how long it is kept, restrictions on use, and the data destruction protocol, disclosed prominently on its website and app. Borrowers may also require deletion of their data. The DPDP erasure rule (Rule 8) applies only to the classes of Data Fiduciary listed in the Third Schedule (e-commerce, online gaming, social media above set user thresholds), so it likely does not apply to this lender directly.
findings.recommendation: Publish a data retention and destruction policy that states contact-list data is not collected. Purge any contact data already held. Verify with counsel whether any DPDP Third Schedule class applies to the business.

findings.document: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025
findings.obligation: A DPDP notice to a Data Principal must be understandable on its own and itemise the personal data and the specific purposes of processing, so that consent is specific and informed. It must also say how consent can be withdrawn, how rights can be exercised and how to complain to the Board. The contacts' details would be collected without any such notice to them.
findings.recommendation: Stop collecting third-party contact data. Where personal data is collected, give DPDP-compliant notices that itemise the data and purposes and explain withdrawal and complaint routes. Seek legal review of third-party data principals.

findings.document: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025
findings.obligation: The NBFC must have a comprehensive, publicly available privacy policy that complies with applicable law and RBI guidelines, and must disclose in it the third parties allowed to collect personal information through the app.
findings.recommendation: Review the privacy policy and app disclosures so they match actual data practices. Remove any reference to contact-list access or contact-based recovery.

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

Our digital lending app asks for permission to read the borrower's phone contacts at sign-up. If a loan becomes overdue, our recovery team calls and messages people in the contact list to remind them that the borrower owes us money.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Are regulated entities and their digital lending apps permitted to access a borrower's phone contacts at onboarding, or are DLA permissions limited to what is needed with the borrower's explicit consent?
- **q2** Is it permitted for a lender's recovery team to contact persons in the borrower's contact list, who are not guarantors or co-obligors, about the borrower's overdue loan?
- **q3** What restrictions apply to the timing, frequency and content of recovery calls and messages, and to disclosure of the borrower's debt to others?
- **q4** Under the DPDP Rules and Act, what notice and consent are required to collect and process the personal data of a borrower's contacts (third-party data principals), and can it be used for recovery?
- **q5** Does the DPDP framework require purpose limitation, data minimisation and erasure of contact-list data collected at sign-up, and what applies once the purpose is no longer served?
- **q6** What do the digital lending directions require on borrower consent for data collection, disclosure of data collected, and the borrower's right to withdraw consent or have data deleted?

## Findings (6)

### 1. [HIGH] An NBFC must ensure its digital lending app (and its LSP's app) collects only need-based data with prior, explicit, auditable borrower consent, and must make the app desist from accessing the contact list, call logs, telephony functions and similar phone resources. Only one-time access to camera, microphone or location is allowed, for onboarding/KYC, with explicit consent.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Remove the contacts permission from the app and any LSP app. Do not read or store the contact list at sign-up, even with the borrower's consent. Delete any contact data already collected. Limit one-time permissions to onboarding/KYC needs.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 13, pp. 19-20 (passage 1728)

### 2. [HIGH] An NBFC and its agents must not harass or intimidate any person in debt collection, including acts that humiliate publicly or intrude on the privacy of the debtor's family members, referees and friends, or sending inappropriate messages by mobile or social media. Contacting people in the borrower's phone contacts to tell them the borrower owes money is such an intrusion.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: Stop recovery calls and messages to contact-list persons who are not guarantors or co-obligors. Limit recovery communications to the borrower and legally bound parties. Train and monitor recovery staff and agents accordingly.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 100, pp. 28-29 (passage 2158)

### 3. [HIGH] Borrowers must be able to give or deny consent for specific data, restrict disclosure to third parties, set retention, revoke consent already given, and have the NBFC/LSP delete their data. The purpose of consent must be disclosed at every stage, and explicit consent is needed before sharing personal information with third parties, unless a statute or regulation requires the sharing.

- Question: q6
- Recommendation: Remove the bulk contacts permission. Give borrowers granular consent, revocation and deletion controls. State the purpose of each data request at every stage. Obtain explicit consent before sharing data with any third party. Do not use sign-up consent as a basis for contacting third parties about debt.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 13, pp. 19-20 (passage 1728)

### 4. [MEDIUM] A DPDP notice to a Data Principal must be understandable on its own and itemise the personal data and the specific purposes of processing, so that consent is specific and informed. It must also say how consent can be withdrawn, how rights can be exercised and how to complain to the Board. The contacts' details would be collected without any such notice to them.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Stop collecting third-party contact data. Where personal data is collected, give DPDP-compliant notices that itemise the data and purposes and explain withdrawal and complaint routes. Seek legal review of third-party data principals.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 3, pp. 24-25 (passage 1962)

### 5. [MEDIUM] The NBFC must have clear data-storage policy guidelines covering the type of data stored, how long it is kept, restrictions on use, and the data destruction protocol, disclosed prominently on its website and app. Borrowers may also require deletion of their data. The DPDP erasure rule (Rule 8) applies only to the classes of Data Fiduciary listed in the Third Schedule (e-commerce, online gaming, social media above set user thresholds), so it likely does not apply to this lender directly.

- Question: q5
- Recommendation: Publish a data retention and destruction policy that states contact-list data is not collected. Purge any contact data already held. Verify with counsel whether any DPDP Third Schedule class applies to the business.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 14, p. 20 (passage 1729)
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 8, part 1 of 2, p. 27 (passage 1967)

### 6. [LOW] The NBFC must have a comprehensive, publicly available privacy policy that complies with applicable law and RBI guidelines, and must disclose in it the third parties allowed to collect personal information through the app.

- Question: q6
- Recommendation: Review the privacy policy and app disclosures so they match actual data practices. Remove any reference to contact-list access or contact-based recovery.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 15, pp. 20-21 (passage 1730)

judge.actionable_reason: The recommendations are generally specific and actionable. Key actions are clear: move data to India-located servers (finding 1), verify storage policies exist and are published (finding 2), confirm consent controls extend to cloud data (finding 3), review LSP contracts and due diligence (finding 4), implement security controls including encryption and logging (finding 6), ensure breach notification processes meet timelines (finding 7), verify KYC retrieval and retention on cloud (finding 8), and check FIU confidentiality protections (finding 9). However, finding 5's recommendation to "monitor any Central Government orders" is somewhat generic and passive rather than a concrete product action. Finding 4's recommendation to "treat the DPDP transfer allowance as no cure" is more of a legal interpretation than a specific product team action. These minor issues prevent a perfect score, but most recommendations are concrete enough for a product team to execute.
judge.grounded_reason: Most findings are well-supported by the passages. The core obligation about India-only storage (finding 1) is directly stated in passage 1729(4). Findings on LSP due diligence (1719), consent and data collection (1728), security safeguards (1965), breach notification (1966), and record retention (1616) are all clearly supported. However, finding 5 on DPDP transfers creates some ambiguity: passage 1978 permits transfers "subject to requirements the Central Government may specify," but the memo's characterization that this "sits alongside the stricter RBI localisation requirement" and that "the stricter sectoral rule governs" is interpretive reasoning not explicitly stated in the passages. The passages do not directly compare or rank these two regimes. Additionally, finding 2's statement that LSPs must not store data "beyond basic minimal data" is supported, but the memo's recommendation to "check whether the app or any LSP holds more than minimal borrower data" assumes the current setup violates this—which the passages support but the memo presents as uncertain.

1616.heading: Chapter VII – Record Management
1616.text:
47. The NBFC shall take the following steps regarding maintenance,
preservation and reporting of customer information, with reference to provisions of
PML Act and Rules. The NBFC shall,
(1) maintain all necessary records of transactions between the NBFC and the
customer, both domestic and international, for at least five years from the date of
transaction;
(2) preserve the records pertaining to the identification of the customers and their
addresses, obtained while opening the account and during the course of business
relationship, for at least five years after the business relationship has ended;
(3) swiftly make available, the identification records and transaction data to the
competent authorities upon request;
(4) introduce a system of maintaining proper records of transactions prescribed
under Rule 3 of Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules,
2005 (PML Rules, 2005);
(5) maintain all necessary information in respect of transactions prescribed under
PML Rule 3 to permit the reconstruction of an individual transaction, including the
following:
(i) the nature of the transactions;
(ii) the amount of the transaction and the currency in which it was denominated;
(iii) the date on which the transaction was conducted; and
(iv) the parties to the transaction.
(6) evolve a system for proper maintenance and preservation of account
information in a manner that allows the NBFC to retrieve data easily and quickly
whenever required or when competent authorities request it;
(7) maintain records of the identity and address of its customers, and records in
respect of transactions referred to in Rule 3 in hard or soft format.
Explanation: For the purpose of this paragraph, the expressions ‘records
pertaining to the identification’, ‘identification records’, etc., shall include
updated records of the identification data, account files, business correspondence,
and results of any analysis undertaken.

1719.heading: Chapter III – Digital Lending › A. General Requirements for NBFC-LSP Arrangements
1719.text:
6. Due diligence requirements with respect to LSPs
(1) Digital lending by an NBFC involving a LSP, shall be carried out under a
contractual agreement between the NBFC and the LSP, which clearly defines
the respective roles, rights, and obligations of each party thereto.
(2) An NBFC shall conduct enhanced due diligence before they enter into an
agreement with a LSP for digital lending, taking into account LSP’s technical
capabilities, robustness of data privacy policies and storage systems, fairness
in conduct with borrowers, past records of conduct and ability to comply with
all applicable regulations and statutes.
(3) An NBFC shall carry out periodic review of the conduct of the LSP vis-à-vis the
terms of the contractual agreement and shall take appropriate action in the
event of any deviation therefrom.
(4) An NBFC shall lay down, as part of its policy, suitable monitoring mechanisms
for the loan portfolios originated with the support of LSPs.
(5) An NBFC shall impart necessary guidance to LSP acting as a recovery agent,
to discharge their duties responsibly and ensure that LSP complies with the
applicable instructions under Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial
Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, and other
relevant instructions as issued from time to time.
(6) An NBFC shall continue to conform to the extant guidelines on outsourcing (as
specified under Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies –
Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025) and shall ensure that the
LSPs engaged by them and the DLAs (either of the NBFC or of the LSPs
engaged by the NBFC) comply with these Directions.
(7) As an overarching principle, any outsourcing agreement entered into by an
NBFC with an LSP shall in no manner dilute or absolve the NBFC of its
obligations under any statutory or regulatory provision, and the NBFC shall
remain fully responsible and liable for all acts and omissions of the LSP.

14. Storage of data
(1) An NBFC shall ensure that LSP engaged by them do not store personal
information of borrower except some basic minimal data (viz., name, address,
contact details of the customer, etc.) that may be required to carry out their
operations or service within the scope of the NBFC-LSP agreement.
Responsibility regarding data privacy and security of the customer’s personal
information on an ongoing basis shall be that of the NBFC.
(2) An NBFC shall ensure that clear policy guidelines regarding the storage of
customer data including the type of data that can be stored, the length of time
for which data can be stored, restrictions on the use of data, data destruction
protocol, standards for handling security breach, etc., are put in place and also
disclosed by the NBFC and the LSP engaged by the NBFC prominently on
their website and DLA at all times.
(3) An NBFC shall ensure that no biometric data is stored / collected by the NBFC
and LSP, unless allowed under extant statutory guidelines.
(4) An NBFC shall ensure that all data is stored only in servers located within India,
while ensuring compliance with statutory obligations/ regulatory instructions.
Further, in case the data is processed outside India, the same shall be deleted
from servers outside India and brought back to India within 24 hours of
processing.

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

Our digital lending app stores all borrower data, including bank statements and KYC documents, on a cloud region in Singapore to reduce cost.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Do the RBI digital lending rules require that data collected by a lending service provider or regulated entity be stored on servers located in India, or do they allow storage in a cloud region outside India such as Singapore?
- **q2** Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules 2025, what conditions or restrictions apply to transferring or storing borrowers' personal data outside India, and how do sectoral requirements such as RBI's apply alongside them?
- **q3** What reasonable security safeguards must a Data Fiduciary implement for borrower data held on a third-party cloud, such as encryption, access control, logging, and breach detection, under the DPDP Rules 2025?
- **q4** What do the RBI KYC Directions require for how KYC records and customer identification documents are maintained and kept accessible to the regulator, including any location, retention, or confidentiality requirements for them?
- **q5** What requirements apply to collection, storage, and sharing of borrower data by digital lending apps, including consent, purpose limitation, data minimisation, and responsibility for outsourced cloud or service providers?
- **q6** What data retention, erasure, and borrower notice obligations apply to personal data stored on the cloud, including bank statements, once the purpose is served or the loan is closed?

## Findings (10)

### 1. [HIGH] An NBFC must ensure all data is stored only on servers located within India. Data processed outside India must be deleted from foreign servers and brought back to India within 24 hours of processing.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Move all borrower data, including bank statements and KYC documents, to India-located servers or a cloud region in India. Singapore may be used only for transient processing, with deletion and return to India within 24 hours. Cost savings do not justify the current design.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 14, p. 20 (passage 1729)

### 2. [MEDIUM] Personal data may be transferred outside India, subject to requirements the Central Government specifies about making the data available to foreign States or entities under their control. This sits alongside the stricter RBI localisation requirement.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: Treat the DPDP transfer allowance as no cure for the RBI requirement, since the stricter sectoral rule governs. Monitor any Central Government orders on transfers.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 15, p. 30 (passage 1978)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 14, p. 20 (passage 1729)

### 3. [MEDIUM] A Data Fiduciary must take reasonable security safeguards for data it holds, including data handled by a Data Processor. These include encryption or masking, access control, logging and monitoring, backups, one-year log retention, and contractual security provisions with the processor.

- Question: q3
- Recommendation: Confirm the cloud setup has encryption, access controls, logging and monitoring, backups, one-year log retention, and security terms in the cloud provider contract.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 6, p. 26 (passage 1965)

### 4. [MEDIUM] The NBFC must preserve identification and transaction records for at least five years. It must retrieve them easily and quickly, and swiftly make them available to competent authorities on request.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Ensure KYC documents on the Singapore cloud can be retrieved promptly for regulators and retained for at least five years. Moving them to India also resolves the localisation issue under the RBI digital lending rules.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 47, pp. 48-49 (passage 1616)

### 5. [MEDIUM] The NBFC must ensure that LSPs do not store borrower personal information beyond basic minimal data. It stays responsible for data privacy and security. It must also have and prominently disclose a data storage policy covering data types, retention period, use restrictions, destruction protocol and breach handling.

- Question: q5
- Recommendation: Check whether the app or any LSP holds more than minimal borrower data on the Singapore cloud. Confirm the storage policy exists and is published on the website and the DLA.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 14, p. 20 (passage 1729)

### 6. [MEDIUM] Outsourcing to an LSP or provider must not dilute the NBFC's obligations. The NBFC remains fully liable, must do enhanced due diligence on LSP storage systems, and must follow outsourcing guidelines.

- Question: q5
- Recommendation: Review the cloud and LSP contracts and the due diligence on their storage systems. Confirm they require India-located storage and cover monitoring and periodic review.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 6, p. 14 (passage 1719)

### 7. [LOW] On becoming aware of a personal data breach, the Data Fiduciary must notify affected Data Principals without delay. It must notify the Board without delay and give detailed information within 72 hours.

- Question: q3
- Recommendation: Make sure the cloud provider is contractually bound to report breaches quickly, and that internal processes can meet the borrower and Board notification timelines.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 7, p. 26 (passage 1966)

### 8. [LOW] The NBFC and its staff must keep confidential the fact that records are maintained and that information is furnished to the FIU Director.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Check that the cloud provider and its personnel cannot access or disclose records and reporting information relating to FIU filings.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 52, pp. 50-51 (passage 1621)

### 9. [LOW] Data collection by the DLA must be need-based and made with prior, explicit consent that has an audit trail. Borrowers must be able to give or deny consent, restrict disclosure, and revoke consent and have data deleted. Explicit consent is required before sharing personal information with third parties.

- Question: q5
- Recommendation: Verify that consent, purpose disclosure and deletion controls extend to data held on the cloud. Check that cloud provider access is covered by consent or a regulatory exception.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 13, pp. 19-20 (passage 1728)

### 10. [LOW] Certain classes of Data Fiduciaries must erase personal data when the specified purpose is no longer served, unless retention is required by law. They must give the Data Principal at least 48 hours' notice before erasure.

- Question: q6
- Recommendation: Check whether the lending app falls in a class listed in the Third Schedule. Either way, set retention and erasure schedules for cloud data, bearing in mind the five-year KYC retention requirement.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 8, part 1 of 2, p. 27 (passage 1967)

## Research limits reached

- q5: stopped after 4 research turns.
- Tool-call budget (20) reached; research stopped before q6.

judge.actionable_reason: All recommendations are specific, correct, and actionable. (1) Stop disbursing into LSP pool account and disburse directly to borrower's bank account—clear operational change. (2) Remove LSP fee deduction and amend LSP agreement so NBFC pays fees from its own funds—specific contractual and payment flow change. (3) Review LSP contract, add contractual prohibitions on fund handling, add periodic checks of LSP fund flows, take corrective action—concrete governance and monitoring steps. (4) Confirm repayments go directly from borrower to NBFC, not through LSP pool account—specific verification task. (5) Ensure KFS and APR sheet show sanctioned amount, all fees, and net disbursed amount accurately, and review APR reflection once LSP fees are paid by NBFC—specific disclosure and documentation requirements. Each recommendation directly addresses the compliance violation and is implementable by the product and operations teams.
judge.grounded_reason: Every finding is fully supported by the cited passages. Finding 1 (1724): passage 1724(1) explicitly prohibits disbursals to third-party accounts including LSP accounts except for statutory/regulatory mandates, co-lending, or end-use disbursals. Finding 2 (1725): passage 1725(4) states fees payable to LSP must be paid directly by the NBFC and not charged to borrowers separately. Finding 3 (1719): passage 1719(7) establishes NBFC remains fully responsible and liable for all LSP acts and omissions, and 1719(1)-(4) require contracts, due diligence, periodic review, and monitoring. Finding 4 (1724): passage 1724(2)-(3) prohibit pass-through/pool accounts and require direct fund flows not controlled by LSPs. Finding 5 (2082, 2081): passage 2082 shows APR computation must include net disbursed amount after deducting all fees including those payable to third parties routed through NBFC, and passage 2081(3) requires KFS include APR computation sheet.

(1) Digital lending by an NBFC involving a LSP, shall be carried out under a

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

For loans sourced through our lending service provider's app, we disburse the loan amount into the LSP's pool account, and the LSP transfers it to the borrower after deducting its own service fee.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Do the digital lending rules allow an NBFC to disburse a loan into an LSP's pool account or any third-party account, or must disbursal go directly to the borrower's bank account?
- **q2** May an LSP deduct its service fee from the loan amount before the funds reach the borrower, or must the NBFC pay LSP fees from its own funds and not charge the borrower directly through the LSP?
- **q3** How must the Key Facts Statement and the APR present the amount actually disbursed to the borrower, and must any deducted fees or charges be disclosed up front?
- **q4** What are the NBFC's responsibilities for due diligence, oversight and accountability for outsourced LSP activity, including LSP handling of loan funds and fee arrangements?
- **q5** What requirements apply to the loan servicing and repayment flow, including whether repayments must go directly from the borrower's account to the NBFC's account without passing through the LSP?

## Findings (5)

### 1. [HIGH] An NBFC must disburse loans only into the borrower's own bank account (with narrow exceptions such as statutory mandates, co-lending flows, and end-use disbursals paid directly to the end-beneficiary). It must ensure no disbursal goes to a third-party account, including an LSP's account.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Stop disbursing into the LSP's pool account. Disburse directly into the borrower's bank account, and confirm that none of the listed exceptions is being relied on. Also ensure the LSP has no direct or indirect control over the flow of funds.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 10, part 1 of 2, pp. 17-18 (passage 1724)

### 2. [HIGH] Fees, charges and reimbursements payable to the LSP must be paid directly by the NBFC. The LSP must not charge or collect them from borrowers separately, so deducting the LSP's fee from the loan amount before it reaches the borrower is not permitted.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: Remove the LSP's deduction from the loan proceeds. Amend the LSP agreement so the NBFC pays LSP fees from its own funds, and make sure no fee is collected from the borrower by the LSP.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 10, part 2 of 2, p. 18 (passage 1725)

### 3. [HIGH] The NBFC must have a contract with the LSP defining roles and obligations, and must conduct enhanced due diligence on the LSP. It must periodically review the LSP's conduct and act on deviations, and it must monitor LSP-originated portfolios. It remains fully responsible and liable for all acts and omissions of the LSP, including its handling of funds.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Review the LSP contract and its monitoring. The pool-account and fee-deduction arrangement shows a deviation that the NBFC's oversight should have caught. Add contractual prohibitions on handling loan funds, add periodic checks of LSP fund flows, and take corrective action. The NBFC remains liable for the LSP's acts.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 6, p. 14 (passage 1719)

### 4. [MEDIUM] The KFS must include an APR computation sheet, with the net disbursed amount shown after deducting fees and charges (including those payable to third parties routed through the NBFC). The APR is computed on the net disbursed amount and includes all charges levied by the NBFC, so deductions must be disclosed up front.

- Question: q3
- Recommendation: Make sure the KFS and APR sheet show the sanctioned amount, all fees and the net disbursed amount accurately. An undisclosed LSP deduction would make the net disbursed amount and APR shown to the borrower wrong. Once LSP fees are paid by the NBFC, check how they are reflected in the APR.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 29, part 2 of 3, pp. 11-12 (passage 2082)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 29, part 1 of 3, pp. 10-11 (passage 2081)

### 5. [MEDIUM] All loan servicing and repayment must be made by the borrower directly into the NBFC's bank account, without any pass-through or pool account of a third party such as the LSP. The flow of funds between the borrower's and the NBFC's accounts must not be controlled directly or indirectly by the LSP.

- Question: q5
- Recommendation: Confirm that repayments go directly from the borrower's account to the NBFC's account and not through the LSP's pool account. Since the LSP already holds a pool account in the disbursal flow, check that it has no control over repayment flows either.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 10, part 1 of 2, pp. 17-18 (passage 1724)

judge.actionable_reason: The recommendations are specific and mostly actionable. Finding 1 clearly directs removal of the no-cancellation rule and addition of a cooling-off period with specified terms. Finding 2 provides a decision tree (check rate type, borrower type, purpose, date, NBFC layer, ticket size, microfinance status) to determine if the charge applies, which is concrete. Finding 3 specifies disclosure locations and timing. Finding 4 recommends reviewing the charge against policy and reasonableness principles, which is somewhat less specific than the others but still actionable as a governance review. A product team could act on all four recommendations, though Finding 4 requires some judgment about what constitutes 'reasonable' scaling or waiver.
judge.grounded_reason: The findings are largely well-supported by the passages. Finding 1 on cooling-off is directly supported by passage 1726. Findings 2 and 3 on pre-payment charges and disclosure are well-grounded in passages 2091, 2090, 2139, 2092, and 2081. Finding 4 on reasonableness is supported by passages 2085 and 2086, though the memo correctly notes these passages do not set a specific fairness test for foreclosure charges. One minor issue: the memo characterizes the 3% charge as a 'foreclosure charge' and 'pre-payment charge' interchangeably, but the passages distinguish between pre-payment charges (regulated) and penal charges (also regulated). The memo's framing of the charge as potentially both types creates slight ambiguity, though the core obligations cited are accurate.

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

Once a digital loan is disbursed it cannot be cancelled. A borrower who wants to exit early pays the full foreclosure charge of 3% of the principal, even on the day after disbursal.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Must a digital loan borrower be given a cooling-off or look-up period during which they can exit the loan by repaying the principal and proportionate APR without any penalty, and does a rule that the loan cannot be cancelled after disbursal comply with this?
- **q2** Are NBFCs restricted from levying foreclosure charges or pre-payment penalties on certain loans, such as floating rate loans to individual borrowers, and is a 3% foreclosure charge on principal permissible for this loan?
- **q3** Must foreclosure or pre-payment charges be disclosed upfront in the Key Facts Statement and loan agreement before the borrower accepts the loan, and what must be disclosed about them?
- **q4** Are charges that are levied immediately after disbursal, such as a full 3% foreclosure fee on the day after disbursal, subject to requirements of fairness, transparency, or being reasonable and not unduly punitive under the responsible business conduct rules?

## Findings (4)

### 1. [HIGH] A digital loan borrower must be given an explicit option to exit the loan during a cooling-off period of at least one day by paying the principal and proportionate APR without any penalty. The NBFC may keep only a reasonable one-time processing fee, disclosed upfront in the KFS.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Remove the rule that a disbursed loan cannot be cancelled. Add an explicit cooling-off exit of at least one day, charging only principal, proportionate APR and any disclosed reasonable one-time processing fee. Do not apply the 3% foreclosure charge during that window.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 11, p. 18 (passage 1726)

### 2. [MEDIUM] For loans sanctioned or renewed on or after 1 January 2026, no pre-payment charges may be levied on floating rate loans to individuals for non-business purposes. The same applies to floating rate business loans to individuals and MSEs for NBFC-UL, and for NBFC-ML up to ₹50 lakh. Existing floating rate non-business term loans to individuals are also barred from pre-payment charges. In other cases, charges follow the approved policy and are based on the amount prepaid. Microfinance loans carry no pre-payment charge.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: Check the loan's rate type (floating or fixed), borrower type, purpose, sanction date, NBFC layer and ticket size, and whether it is a microfinance loan. If a prohibition applies, remove the 3% charge. Otherwise, make sure the charge is in the Board-approved policy and is levied on the amount prepaid.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 34, part 1 of 2, pp. 17-18 (passage 2091)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 33, p. 17 (passage 2090)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 81, p. 26 (passage 2139)

### 3. [MEDIUM] Whether pre-payment charges apply must be clearly disclosed in the sanction letter and loan agreement, and in the KFS where one is required. Any pre-payment charge not disclosed in this way cannot be levied. No charges waived earlier may be levied retrospectively at pre-payment.

- Question: q3
- Recommendation: Disclose the 3% foreclosure charge in the sanction letter, loan agreement and KFS before the borrower accepts the loan. Include it in the APR computation, and do not charge anything undisclosed. Also disclose any one-time processing fee retained on cooling-off exit.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 34, part 2 of 2, p. 18 (passage 2092)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 29, part 1 of 3, pp. 10-11 (passage 2081)

### 4. [LOW] Charges must be transparent and disclosed upfront. The penal charge provisions require charges to be reasonable and commensurate, and not a revenue enhancement tool. The passages do not set a fairness test for foreclosure charges specifically. A full 3% charge the day after disbursal is worth reviewing against these principles and the interest-rate and charges policy.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Review whether charging the full 3% on day one is consistent with the Board-approved charges policy and the reasonableness principles. Consider scaling or waiving the charge for very early exit.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 30, part 2 of 3, p. 14 (passage 2085)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025, Para 30, part 3 of 3, pp. 14-15 (passage 2086)

## Research limits reached

- q4: stopped after 4 research turns.

judge.actionable_reason: The recommendations are specific and mostly correct. Finding 1 provides concrete steps: replace the 30-day timeline with 'without delay,' prepare a template covering five elements, and use registered channels—all actionable. Finding 2 specifies removing the 'no regulator' stance, adding Board notification steps, assigning owners, preparing templates, and requesting extensions if needed—specific and implementable. Finding 3 recommends documenting logging, monitoring, one-year retention, encryption, access controls, backups, and processor clauses, plus integrating breach detection into the incident plan—all concrete. Finding 4 appropriately conditions recommendations on whether the feature touches digital lending and recommends documenting the plan in the data storage policy, publishing it, extending to LSPs, and aligning with RBI standards—specific and fitting. The only minor limitation is that Finding 4's recommendation depends on clarifying whether this NBFC operates a digital lending platform, which adds a conditional element, but this is appropriate given the feature description does not explicitly state this context.
judge.grounded_reason: Every finding is fully supported by the cited passages. Finding 1 cites Rule 7(1) of passage 1966, which explicitly requires notification 'without delay' with all five specified content elements—the memo correctly identifies this contradicts the 30-day post-investigation plan. Finding 2 cites Rule 7(2) of passage 1966, which mandates Board notification 'without delay' and a detailed 72-hour report—the memo accurately reflects these obligations absent from the current plan. Finding 3 cites passages 1965 and 1968, which detail reasonable security safeguards including encryption, access controls, logging, monitoring, one-year log retention, backups, and processor contracts—all correctly summarized. Finding 4 cites passages 1729 and 1731, which require NBFCs to have documented breach-handling standards in their data storage policy, disclose them publicly, extend them to LSPs, and comply with RBI cybersecurity standards—all accurately represented. No claims exceed what the passages state.

6. Reasonable security safeguards. — (1) A Data Fiduciary shall protect personal data in its possession or
under its control, including in respect of any processing undertaken by it or on its behalf by a Data
Processor, by taking reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breach, which shall include, at

(b) appropriate measures to control access to the computer resources used by such Data Fiduciary or
such a Data Processor, wherever applicable;
(c) visibility on the accessing of such personal data, through appropriate logs, monitoring and review,
for enabling detection of unauthorised access, its investigation and remediation to prevent
recurrence;
(d) reasonable measures for continued processing in the event of confidentiality, integrity or
availability of such personal data being compromised as a result of destruction or loss of access to
personal data or otherwise, such as by way of data-backups;

recurrence and continued processing in the event of such a compromise, retain such logs and
personal data for a period of one year, unless compliance with any law for the time being in force
requires otherwise;
(f) appropriate provision in the contract entered into between such Data Fiduciary and such a Data
Processor, wherever applicable, for taking reasonable security safeguards; and
(g) appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure effective observance of security
safeguards.

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

If our customer database is breached, our incident plan is to email affected customers within 30 days once the investigation is complete. We do not plan to inform any regulator or board.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Under the DPDP Rules 2025, must a data fiduciary notify affected data principals of a personal data breach, and what timing, content and manner of intimation is required?
- **q2** Under the DPDP Rules 2025, must a data fiduciary notify the Data Protection Board of a personal data breach, and within what deadlines (initial and detailed report)?
- **q3** Does the DPDP Act and Rules require a data fiduciary to maintain reasonable security safeguards and breach detection, investigation and log retention to prevent and respond to personal data breaches?
- **q4** Do the RBI Directions for NBFCs require reporting of a data breach or cyber incident involving customer data to the RBI, and what timelines apply?
- **q5** Do the RBI Directions for NBFCs require incidents involving customer data to be escalated to the board or its committees, and what governance oversight of data security is expected?
- **q6** Do the RBI digital lending provisions in the NBFC Credit Facilities Directions impose data security, storage and breach-related obligations on the NBFC and its lending service providers that affect the incident plan?

## Findings (4)

### 1. [HIGH] On becoming aware of a personal data breach, the Data Fiduciary must intimate each affected Data Principal without delay, in a concise, clear and plain manner, through her user account or registered communication mode. The notice must describe the breach, its consequences, mitigation measures, safety steps the person can take, and a business contact.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Replace the 'within 30 days after the investigation' plan with notification without delay once the company becomes aware of the breach. Do not wait for the investigation to finish. Use a template that covers all five required content elements (nature/extent/timing, consequences, mitigation, safety measures, contact) and send it through the registered channel or user account.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 7, p. 26 (passage 1966)

### 2. [HIGH] The Data Fiduciary must intimate the Data Protection Board of any personal data breach without delay, with a description of nature, extent, timing, location and likely impact. It must then give a detailed report within 72 hours of becoming aware (or a longer period the Board allows), including facts, mitigation, findings on the cause, remedial measures and a report on intimations to Data Principals.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: Remove the 'no regulator' stance. Add steps to notify the Board without delay and to file the detailed 72-hour report. Assign owners, prepare templates, and keep the option of a written request to the Board for a longer period.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 7, p. 26 (passage 1966)

### 3. [MEDIUM] The Data Fiduciary must take reasonable security safeguards to prevent breaches. These include encryption or masking, access controls, logs and monitoring to detect unauthorised access and support investigation and remediation, backups for continued processing, retention of logs and personal data for one year, processor contract terms, and appropriate technical and organisational measures.

- Question: q3
- Recommendation: The plan describes only post-breach emailing and shows no detection, investigation, log retention or backup controls. Confirm and document logging and monitoring, one-year log retention, encryption, access control, backups and processor contract clauses. Make breach detection and investigation part of the incident plan.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 6, p. 26 (passage 1965)
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 8, part 2 of 2, p. 27 (passage 1968)

### 4. [MEDIUM] The NBFC remains responsible for data privacy and security of borrowers' personal information. It must have clear policy guidelines on data storage, including standards for handling security breaches, and disclose them on its website and digital lending app. It must also ensure that it and its lending service providers comply with RBI cybersecurity technology standards.

- Question: q6
- Recommendation: If the feature touches digital lending, make sure the incident plan is a documented breach-handling standard within the data storage policy. Publish it on the website and app, and extend it to lending service providers. Align it with RBI cybersecurity standards, since the current plan of delayed customer-only notice and no regulator or board involvement is unlikely to meet them.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 14, p. 20 (passage 1729)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 16, p. 21 (passage 1731)

## Research limits reached

- q2: stopped after 4 research turns.

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

We are launching a pocket-money card and app for teenagers aged 13 to 17. They sign up themselves with their name, date of birth and phone number; parents are not involved.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Does the DPDP Act and Rules 2025 require verifiable consent of a parent or lawful guardian before processing the personal data of a child under 18, and can a teenager aged 13 to 17 sign up alone without parental involvement?
- **q2** What methods must a data fiduciary use to verify that a person is an adult parent of the child and to ascertain the age of the user, under the DPDP Rules 2025?
- **q3** Do the DPDP Rules restrict tracking, behavioural monitoring or targeted advertising directed at children, and what exemptions apply to a financial service provider?
- **q4** Can an NBFC onboard a minor as a customer and issue a card or prepaid payment instrument to them, and what KYC (customer due diligence) is required for a minor, including the role of a guardian?
- **q5** Under the NBFC Credit Facilities Directions, including digital lending, can credit be extended to a person below 18 years, and must a minor have legal capacity to enter a loan or credit card contract?
- **q6** What disclosures under the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, such as key facts statement, fees and charges, and grievance redressal, must be given to a minor customer or their guardian before the product is used?

## Findings (1)

### 1. [HIGH] A Data Fiduciary must adopt technical and organisational measures to obtain verifiable consent of the parent before processing any personal data of a child, and must check that the person claiming to be the parent is an identifiable adult.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Do not let 13 to 17 year olds sign up alone. Add a parent or guardian consent step before any personal data (name, date of birth, phone number) is processed.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 10, part 1 of 3, pp. 27-28 (passage 1970)

judge.actionable_reason: The recommendations are generally specific and actionable for a product team. Finding 1 recommends redacting/masking the first 8 digits before storage and purging existing unmasked copies—specific and implementable. Finding 2 recommends defining a five-year retention schedule followed by deletion, with masked storage—clear and actionable. Finding 3 recommends switching to self-declaration or Aadhaar OTP e-KYC and checking Board policy—specific. Finding 4 recommends setting erasure timelines tied to KYC retention and notifying customers—actionable. Finding 5 recommends encryption, role-based access controls, logging, and contract terms—specific and implementable. Finding 6 recommends restricting access through authenticated application with audit trails and checking cloud arrangements—mostly actionable but slightly generic on 'check cloud storage arrangements.' Overall the recommendations are concrete enough for product implementation, though some could be more prescriptive on technical implementation details.
judge.grounded_reason: Most findings are well-supported by the passages. Finding 1 (HIGH) is clearly grounded in passages 1579 and 1590 requiring masking/blackout of Aadhaar numbers. Finding 2 (MEDIUM) is supported by passage 1616 on five-year retention after relationship ends. Finding 3 (MEDIUM) is grounded in passages 1606-1608 showing re-KYC can use self-declaration or Aadhaar OTP, not stored images. Finding 4 (MEDIUM) is supported by passages 1967-1968 on data erasure timelines. Finding 5 (HIGH) is grounded in passage 1965 on security safeguards. Finding 6 (MEDIUM) is supported by passages 1580 and 1728 on authenticated application access and need-based data collection. However, passage 1580 is incomplete (cuts off mid-sentence at 'shall control the access to the'), so the full scope of the digital KYC access control requirement cannot be fully verified from the provided text.

1606.text:
42. Updation / Periodic Updation of KYC
(1) The NBFC shall adopt a risk-based approach for periodic updation of KYC
ensuring that it keeps the information or data collected under CDD is kept up-to-date
and relevant, particularly where there is high risk. However, the NBFC shall carry out
periodic updation at least once in every two years for high-risk customers, once in
every eight years for medium risk customers and once in every 10 years for low-risk
customers from the date of opening of the account / last KYC updation. The NBFC
shall document its policy in this regard as part of the NBFC’s internal KYC policy duly
approved by the Board of Directors of NBFC or any committee of the Board to which
power has been delegated.
(2) Notwithstanding the provisions given above, in respect of an individual
customer who is categorised as low-risk, the NBFC shall allow all transactions and
ensure the updation of KYC within one year of its falling due for KYC or up to June 30,
2026, whichever is later. The NBFC shall subject accounts of such customers to
regular monitoring. This shall also apply to low-risk individual customers for whom
periodic updation of KYC has already fallen due.
(3) Individuals:
(i) No change in KYC information: In case of no change in the KYC information,
the NBFC shall obtain a self-declaration from the customer in this regard through the
customer’s email-id registered with the NBFC, customer’s mobile number registered
with the NBFC, digital channels (including mobile application of NBFC) letter, etc.

1616.document_title: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025
1616.heading: Chapter VII – Record Management
1616.text:
47. The NBFC shall take the following steps regarding maintenance,
preservation and reporting of customer information, with reference to provisions of
PML Act and Rules. The NBFC shall,
(1) maintain all necessary records of transactions between the NBFC and the
customer, both domestic and international, for at least five years from the date of
transaction;
(2) preserve the records pertaining to the identification of the customers and their
addresses, obtained while opening the account and during the course of business
relationship, for at least five years after the business relationship has ended;
(3) swiftly make available, the identification records and transaction data to the
competent authorities upon request;
(4) introduce a system of maintaining proper records of transactions prescribed
under Rule 3 of Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules,
2005 (PML Rules, 2005);
(5) maintain all necessary information in respect of transactions prescribed under
PML Rule 3 to permit the reconstruction of an individual transaction, including the
following:
(i) the nature of the transactions;
(ii) the amount of the transaction and the currency in which it was denominated;
(iii) the date on which the transaction was conducted; and
(iv) the parties to the transaction.
(6) evolve a system for proper maintenance and preservation of account
information in a manner that allows the NBFC to retrieve data easily and quickly
whenever required or when competent authorities request it;
(7) maintain records of the identity and address of its customers, and records in
respect of transactions referred to in Rule 3 in hard or soft format.
Explanation: For the purpose of this paragraph, the expressions ‘records
pertaining to the identification’, ‘identification records’, etc., shall include
updated records of the identification data, account files, business correspondence,
and results of any analysis undertaken.

1965.text:
6. Reasonable security safeguards. — (1) A Data Fiduciary shall protect personal data in its possession or
under its control, including in respect of any processing undertaken by it or on its behalf by a Data
Processor, by taking reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breach, which shall include, at
the minimum, —
(a) appropriate data security measures, such as securing of personal data through encryption,
obfuscation, masking or the use of virtual tokens mapped to that personal data;
(b) appropriate measures to control access to the computer resources used by such Data Fiduciary or
such a Data Processor, wherever applicable;
(c) visibility on the accessing of such personal data, through appropriate logs, monitoring and review,
for enabling detection of unauthorised access, its investigation and remediation to prevent
recurrence;
(d) reasonable measures for continued processing in the event of confidentiality, integrity or
availability of such personal data being compromised as a result of destruction or loss of access to
personal data or otherwise, such as by way of data-backups;
(e) for enabling the detection of unauthorised access, its investigation, remediation to prevent
recurrence and continued processing in the event of such a compromise, retain such logs and
personal data for a period of one year, unless compliance with any law for the time being in force
requires otherwise;
(f) appropriate provision in the contract entered into between such Data Fiduciary and such a Data
Processor, wherever applicable, for taking reasonable security safeguards; and
(g) appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure effective observance of security
safeguards.
(2) In this rule, the expression “computer resource” shall have the same meaning as is assigned to it in
Information Technology Act, 2000 (21 of 2000).

Principal neither approaches such Data Fiduciary for the performance of the specified purpose nor exercises

(2) At least forty-eight hours before completion of the time period for erasure of personal data under this

completion of such period, unless she logs into her user account or otherwise initiates contact with the Data
Fiduciary for the performance of the specified purpose or exercises her rights in relation to the processing
of such personal data.

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

During onboarding we photograph the customer's Aadhaar card (front and back) and keep the unmasked images in our cloud bucket indefinitely, so that periodic re-KYC can reuse them. Branch staff can download them from the admin portal.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Are NBFCs permitted to collect and retain unmasked Aadhaar card images, or must the Aadhaar number be redacted or blacked out when a copy of the Aadhaar is taken for customer identification?
- **q2** What are the NBFC's record retention requirements and limits for KYC documents and identification records, both during the relationship and after it ends or the account is closed?
- **q3** Can previously collected KYC documents be reused for periodic updation or re-KYC, or must the customer re-submit documents or self-declare any change in details?
- **q4** Under the DPDP Rules 2025, what obligation does a Data Fiduciary have to erase personal data once the specified purpose is no longer served, and what retention limits apply to personal data held indefinitely?
- **q5** What reasonable security safeguards must the NBFC apply to personal data such as Aadhaar images, including encryption, access controls, logging and monitoring of staff access, and breach prevention?
- **q6** Do the KYC Directions or the digital lending rules place conditions on how customer KYC data is stored, who can access it, and where it is held (such as cloud storage), and on the security of KYC records?

## Findings (6)

### 1. [HIGH] Where Aadhaar authentication is not required, the NBFC must ensure the customer blacks out the Aadhaar number, and for V-CIP it must redact or black out the Aadhaar number. Storing unmasked Aadhaar images conflicts with this.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Redact or black out the Aadhaar number (at least the first 8 digits) before the image is stored. Where authentication is not carried out, do not keep the unmasked copy. Purge or mask the images already held.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 23, part 4 of 4, p. 26 (passage 1579)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 27, part 4 of 5, pp. 33-34 (passage 1590)

### 2. [HIGH] A Data Fiduciary must take reasonable security safeguards. At the minimum these are encryption, masking or obfuscation, access controls, logs with monitoring and review of access, backups, and one-year log retention. Unmasked Aadhaar images that any branch staff can download need these controls.

- Question: q5
- Recommendation: Encrypt the bucket, restrict downloads to role-based least-privilege access, and log and review every access. Keep logs for one year and add backups. Include security terms in the cloud provider contract.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 6, p. 26 (passage 1965)

### 3. [MEDIUM] The NBFC must preserve identification and address records for at least five years after the business relationship ends. The Directions set a minimum period, not a licence to hold them indefinitely. Records must be retrievable and made available to authorities on request.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: Define a retention schedule of at least five years after the relationship ends, followed by deletion unless another law requires longer. Keep only the identification records needed, in masked form.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 47, pp. 48-49 (passage 1616)

### 4. [MEDIUM] Periodic updation is done by self-declaration where nothing has changed, and by self-declaration of the new address where only the address has changed. A copy of the OVD is only optional and must be specified in the Board-approved KYC policy. Documents on file must meet current CDD standards, and expired documents require fresh KYC. Reusing stored unmasked Aadhaar images is not the prescribed route.

- Question: q3
- Recommendation: Run re-KYC through self-declaration or Aadhaar OTP e-KYC rather than reusing stored Aadhaar images. Check that the stored documents meet current CDD standards. Record any OVD-copy requirement in the Board-approved KYC policy.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 42, part 1 of 5, pp. 40-41 (passage 1606)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 42, part 2 of 5, pp. 41-42 (passage 1607)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 42, part 3 of 5, pp. 42-43 (passage 1608)

### 5. [MEDIUM] A Data Fiduciary must erase personal data once the specified purpose is no longer served, unless retention is needed to comply with law. It must retain the data and logs for a minimum of one year and then erase them unless another law requires longer. Keeping Aadhaar images indefinitely has no basis beyond the legal retention period.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Set an erasure timeline tied to the KYC retention period, including for the cloud bucket and its backups. Notify customers before erasure where Rule 8 requires it.
- Citations:
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 8, part 2 of 2, p. 27 (passage 1968)
  - Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 8, part 1 of 2, p. 27 (passage 1967)

### 6. [MEDIUM] The Digital KYC process must run only through an authenticated NBFC application, and the NBFC must control access to that application. Under the digital lending directions, data collection must be need-based, with explicit consent and an audit trail. Unrestricted downloads from an admin portal conflict with these controls.

- Question: q6
- Recommendation: Restrict access to KYC images to authorised officers through the authenticated application. Confirm that the data collected is need-based and has an audit trail of consent. Check cloud storage arrangements against the KYC and digital lending requirements.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 24, part 1 of 4, pp. 26-27 (passage 1580)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025, Para 13, pp. 19-20 (passage 1728)

## Research limits reached

- Tool-call budget (20) reached; research stopped before q6.

judge.actionable_reason: All recommendations are specific, technically feasible, and directly address the feature's compliance gap. They specify: (1) introduce periodic KYC updation documented in Board policy; (2) configure risk engine to schedule by category with specific timelines and backlog prioritization; (3) confirm intensified monitoring and link 6-month reviews to enhanced due diligence; (4) build controls for expired documents and address verification within two months; (5) ensure risk categories feed into updation frequency and policy documentation. Each recommendation is concrete enough for a product team to implement and directly remediates the stated non-compliance.
judge.grounded_reason: Every finding is fully supported by the cited passages. Finding 1 correctly cites Para 42(1) which mandates periodic updation at risk-based intervals and prohibits one-time KYC. Finding 2 accurately cites the specific intervals (2/8/10 years) from Para 42(1). Finding 3 is supported by Para 39 (ongoing due diligence) and Para 41 (high-risk intensified monitoring and 6-month review). Finding 4 is supported by Para 42(2) and Para 42(5)(i) regarding expired documents and Para 42(2) regarding address verification within two months. Finding 5 is supported by Para 20 (risk categorisation) and Para 41(1) (6-month periodic review). All obligations stated in findings are explicitly contained in the passages cited.

state.memo:
# Compliance review

## Feature

We complete KYC once at onboarding and never update it afterwards, including for customers our risk engine classifies as high risk.

## Questions researched

- **q1** Does the RBI KYC Directions for NBFCs require periodic updation of KYC for existing customers, and is a one-time KYC at onboarding with no later updation permitted?
- **q2** What is the prescribed frequency of KYC periodic updation for high risk customers, and how does it differ for medium and low risk customers?
- **q3** What ongoing due diligence and transaction monitoring must an NBFC carry out on customers classified as high risk, including enhanced due diligence?
- **q4** What must an NBFC do when customer KYC documents or information become outdated, such as expired identity documents, change of address, or customer non-response to updation requests?
- **q5** Are NBFCs required to have a risk-based KYC policy with periodic review of risk categorisation, and must high risk classification trigger specific actions or senior management involvement?

## Findings (5)

### 1. [HIGH] The NBFC must keep CDD information up to date through periodic updation of KYC, using a risk-based approach, at fixed maximum intervals from account opening or the last updation. A one-time KYC at onboarding with no later updation is not permitted.

- Question: q1
- Recommendation: Introduce a periodic KYC updation process for all customers. Document it in the Board-approved KYC policy and apply it to existing customers who are already overdue.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 42, part 1 of 5, pp. 40-41 (passage 1606)

### 2. [HIGH] Periodic updation is required at least every 2 years for high-risk customers, every 8 years for medium-risk customers and every 10 years for low-risk customers, counted from account opening or the last KYC updation.

- Question: q2
- Recommendation: Configure the risk engine and KYC workflow to schedule updation by risk category: 2 years for high risk, 8 for medium and 10 for low. Clear the backlog of high-risk customers first.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 42, part 1 of 5, pp. 40-41 (passage 1606)

### 3. [MEDIUM] The NBFC must carry out ongoing due diligence so that transactions are consistent with its knowledge of the customer and the customer's risk profile. It must subject high-risk accounts to more intensified monitoring and review risk categorisation at least every six months to decide whether enhanced due diligence is needed.

- Question: q3
- Recommendation: Confirm that high-risk customers receive intensified monitoring and that risk categorisation is reviewed at least every six months. Link the outcome of that review to enhanced due diligence.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 41, p. 40 (passage 1605)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 39, p. 40 (passage 1603)

### 4. [MEDIUM] At periodic updation, the NBFC must hold KYC documents that meet current CDD standards. If the validity of the CDD documents has expired, it must run a KYC process equivalent to onboarding a new customer. It must also handle changes of address through self-declaration and verify the new address within two months.

- Question: q4
- Recommendation: Build controls to detect expired documents and address changes. Trigger fresh KYC for expired documents, and verify declared new addresses within two months.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 42, part 3 of 5, pp. 42-43 (passage 1608)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 42, part 2 of 5, pp. 41-42 (passage 1607)

### 5. [LOW] The NBFC must categorise customers as low, medium or high risk and apply a risk-based approach. It must put a system in place to review risk categorisation at least every six months.

- Question: q5
- Recommendation: Make sure risk categories from the risk engine feed into KYC updation frequency and enhanced due diligence. Ensure the risk categorisation is reviewed periodically and documented in the Board-approved KYC policy.
- Citations:
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 20, p. 21 (passage 1573)
  - Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025, Para 41, p. 40 (passage 1605)

## Research limits reached

- q2: stopped after 4 research turns.
- q4: stopped after 4 research turns.
- q5: stopped after 4 research turns.

judge.actionable_reason: The recommendations are specific and mostly correct. Finding 1's recommendation to show KFS before acceptance with unique proposal number, validity period, explanation, and acknowledgement is specific and actionable. Finding 2's recommendation to present APR and fees in standardized format before acceptance and include KFS summary in agreement is clear and actionable. Finding 3's recommendation to obtain acceptance only after KFS and build in cooling-off exit option is specific and actionable. Finding 4's recommendation about emailing digitally signed documents with KFS and sanction letter is specific, though it could be slightly clearer about the timing requirement (at sanction or disbursement). The recommendations appropriately address the feature's current gap of showing APR and fees only post-acceptance rather than pre-acceptance.
judge.grounded_reason: The findings are largely supported by the passages. Finding 1 correctly cites the KFS requirement before contract execution (2081), the need for APR computation sheet and amortisation schedule (2081, 2083), and the unique proposal number and validity period (2081). Finding 2 accurately reflects that APR must include all charges (2083) and third-party charges must be disclosed separately (2083), and that charges not in KFS cannot be levied without consent (2083). Finding 3 correctly cites the cooling-off period requirement (1726) and the processing fee disclosure (1726). Finding 4 accurately reflects the requirement for digitally signed documents to flow to borrower's email (1722) and the need for written communication in understood language (2062, 2065, 2066). However, there is a minor issue: Finding 1 states the KFS must be 'explained to the borrower, with an acknowledgement obtained' - while 2081 does say 'Contents of KFS shall be explained to the borrower and an acknowledgement shall be obtained,' the passages do not explicitly state this must occur before acceptance in the journey flow, though this is a reasonable interpretation of the requirement.
